title: Load the fast reference
text: G is the detection-efficiency ratio of the two polarisation channels. It is measured on a dye that depolarises within the pulse width, so its true anisotropy is zero in the tail and VV/VH there is G alone. With your own data, load that dye's VV/VH decay here (or drop the file on the window); the example has already loaded the simulated one, and the status line shows the G it gives.

title: Start with references whose answer you know
text: Load example loads simulated references written by the plugin itself: a dye that depolarises within the pulse (the fast reference), a slow protein (rho 16 ns, r0 0.38) and two batch decays. Their VH channel was detected with 1/1.2 the efficiency of VV, so tail matching must give G close to 1.2, and with no polarisation mixing simulated the mixing estimate must come out near zero.

title: Match the tails
text: The yellow lines in the decay plot (and the Tail start / Tail stop fields) mark the region whose ratio gives G. Choose a stretch where the dye has fully depolarised and the decay is still well above the background. Turn on Background correction and set the blue background region when the pre-pulse level matters.

await.hint: Change Tail start (type a bin and press Enter, or use the arrows).

title: Load a slow protein reference
text: A slow-rotating, long-lived reference has a known steady-state anisotropy. Its measured value constrains the polarisation mixing: only the single linked estimate l1 = l2 can be determined from one observable, and values outside 0 to 0.5 are shown but not applied. The example loaded a simulated slow protein; for your own instrument press Slow protein... and choose its file.

title: Export the calibration
text: Check the corrected anisotropy r(t) of both references first: the fast dye should sit near zero in the tail, the slow protein near its Perrin value. Then export the values as JSON or archive them with their provenance.
